[א] [לבוש] וקדושת היום וכו'. ואם לא סידר הקרבנות בתפילת מוסף חוזר אף על פי שלא אמר כאמור כי הוי צורך היום דרשות מהר"ש (מלבושי יום טוב), וצריך עיון מסימן רס"ח סעיף ד':
[ב] [לבוש] לשון סדור וכו'. ובתניא לשון בירור כמו ותוכן לבות ה', עד כאן, יש לומר ואת מוסף וכו' וכן בכל מוסף (רש"ל ס"ד), הא דאומרים בשחרית ולא נתתו ולא הנחלתו לשון זכר משום דקאי על מה דסיים וביום השביעי ויום הוא לשון זכר אבל במוסף דקאי על תכנת שבת ושבת לשון נקבה אומרים קרבנותיה פירושיה, כך שמעתי ממורי מהר"ר הלמן זכרונו לברכה שאמר בשם חמיו, ועיין סימן רצ"ב ס"ק מ' דשבת הוא נמי לשון זכר:
[ג] [לבוש] חבירים וכו'. פירוש שעתיד הקב"ה לעשות סעודה לצדיקים ממנו:
[ד] [לבוש] קריאת שמע וכו'. ה' אחר הוא אלקינו ואין לומר שתי פעמים אחד ומנהג שלנו לומר שתי פעמים אחד (מגן אברהם), ועיין ספר המנהיג סימן מ"ד, ובאבודרהם כתב דלכך מפרש הוא אלקינו ועיין סימן ס"א סעיף ט':
[ה] [לבוש] וטעמא וכו'. ובספר המנהיג כתב זה לשונו אולי בשבת ויום טוב שהיו מרבין בתפילה הרגישו על זה כענין תקיעות שבמוסף, עד כאן. והטעם וכו' עיין סימן תרכ"א, ובמהרי"ל הלכות יום כיפור א'ין מ'י נ'ודה ראשי תיבות אמן ואחר כך ברוך אתה, והוי כאילו אמר ברוך אתה א'ל מ'לך נ'אמן:
eliyah_rabbah.en:
[1] [Levush] And the sanctity of the day, etc. If he did not recite the order of the offerings in the Mussaf prayer, he must repeat the prayer, even if he did not say "as stated," because this is required for the day, as stated in the responsa of Maharam of Rothenburg (Malbushei Yom Tov). This requires study in light of siman 268, seif 4.
[2] [Levush] The expression "arranged," etc. In Tanya it is explained as an expression of clarification, as in, "and He weighs the hearts." One should say "and the Mussaf offering, etc.," and likewise in every Mussaf prayer (Maharshal, siman 64). In Shacharit we say "You did not give it and You did not bequeath it" in the masculine form because it refers back to "and on the seventh day," and "day" is masculine. In Mussaf, however, it refers to the arrangement of Shabbos, and "Shabbos" is feminine, so we say "its offerings" and "its explanations." I heard this from my teacher, Rabbi Helman of blessed memory, who said it in the name of his father in law. See siman 292, seif katan 40, where Shabbos is also treated as masculine.
[3] [Levush] Companions, etc. Meaning that in the future the Holy One, blessed is He, will make a feast for the righteous from it.
[4] [Levush] Shema, etc. "Hashem is One" follows "He is our God," and one should not say "One" twice. Our custom, however, is to say "One" twice (Magen Avraham). See Sefer HaManhig, siman 44. Abudraham writes that for this reason we explain, "He is our God." See siman 61, seif 9.
[5] [Levush] And the reason, etc. Sefer HaManhig writes: Perhaps on Shabbos and Yom Tov, when they prolonged the prayer, they became aware of this, analogous to the shofar blasts in Mussaf. See siman 621 regarding the reason. In Maharil, Hilchot Yom Kippur, the initial letters of "ein mi nodeh" spell amen, followed by "Baruch Atah," so it is as though one said "Baruch Atah El Melech Ne'eman."

machatzit_hashekel.en:
In the writings of the Arizal, etc. ‘Hashem is One; He is our God.’ This means that in Naaritzcha, where the text in the siddurim reads, ‘Shema Yisrael, etc., Hashem is One; One is our God,’ they wrote that one should not say the word ‘One’ twice. The reason is that stated above in siman 61, seif 9: it is prohibited to recite Shema twice, whether one repeats the words, etc., because it appears as though there were, God forbid, two authorities.
Nevertheless, our custom is to say ‘One’ twice. This is not comparable to the case in siman 61, for the first ‘One’ refers to what precedes it, whereas the final ‘One’ refers to what follows it.
And the Mussaf offering, etc. With the conjunction ‘and.’ Maharshal concludes: ‘For it refers back to what precedes it.’ This concludes his words.

And it must be explained, etc. For Mincha can be made up, etc. By chance I saw in Tzelach on Berachos, by our master Rabbi Yechezkel, of blessed memory, Av Beis Din of the holy community of Prague, that he wrote that Magen Avraham overlooked the words of the Jerusalem Talmud, where the opposite of his position is explained: when there is insufficient time, it is even more evident that Mincha takes precedence; see there. Or, when he does not have so much wine, one may rely on the poskim who hold that it suffices for him to drink the entire kiddush cup, which holds a revi'it, for this is also called kiddush in the place of a meal.

It appears that if his heart is weak, he may also eat bread until his mind is settled, even if it is more than a kebeitzah. Eliyah Rabbah wrote, and it is brought in Shaarei Teshuvah, that if his heart is weak and he has no wine or other item on which to make kiddush, he may eat fruit, and the same applies to types of targima from the five species, before Mussaf even without kiddush; but otherwise one should not be lenient.
